USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the existing Section 301 tariffs in place and use the already-scheduled Trump–Xi G20 meeting to reopen talks, without a new tariff hike and without a rollback. Treat the January 1, 2019 step-up of List 3 from 10% to 25% as leverage to extract a work plan on IP, forced tech transfer, and industrial subsidies—not as an automatic next shot. Do not trade structural demands for another purchases-only truce of the May 19 type; do not add the remaining ~$260B list before Buenos Aires.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not high. Combined US coverage is now ~$250B of Chinese imports (Lists 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% from Sept 24), and China has answered with matching $50B plus 5–10% on ~$60B of US goods. That retaliation is already biting a core US export sector: US goods exports to China fell about 20% from June to November (EXPCH $10.86B to $8.65B), and federal data through mid-October show US soybean sales to China down 94%, with cash prices in the farm belt below $7/bu versus nearly $10 a year earlier and USDA aid covering less than half of estimated losses. The original 301 problem is also still live: the March 22 USTR findings on IP and tech transfer have not been remedied, and late-October comments from Kudlow and others were that Beijing had still not answered on those structural items. That combination sits well below the +0.5 US anchor (national GDP drag is not yet material). US industrial production is still rising, Michigan sentiment remains high at 97.5, and CPI is contained; Moody's public estimate of a ~0.2pp US growth hit is modest next to China's 0.3–0.5pp. The US still has leverage—CNY has weakened ~9% toward 6.92, China IP growth has cooled, and Xi agreed on Nov 1 to a G20 meeting—but October VIX spikes above 25, a stronger dollar, and rising Fed funds (2.20%) mean the US economy has less spare room to absorb a further shock. Action should therefore stay near hold/negotiate. Escalating now (List 3 to 25% early, or the remaining ~$260B list floated in late October) would hit consumer goods and supply chains, deepen farm-belt losses before Brazil's spring harvest, and poison the only live leader-level channel. Rolling back or locking in purchase commitments would repeat May 19–29, when a purchases joint statement was walked back within ten days and produced no structural movement. Midterms (Democrats taking the House, GOP Senate) do not constrain unilateral tariff authority and are bipartisan-hawkish on China, so there is no domestic need to concede—and no excuse to skip the G20 window.
key_factors: Section 301 now covers ~$250B of Chinese imports, with List 3 scheduled to rise from 10% to 25% on Jan 1, 2019
China retaliation has crushed a key US export sector: EXPCH -20% since June; soybean sales to China -94% through mid-October
Core 301 grievances (IP, forced tech transfer, industrial policy) remain unaddressed; May purchases truce collapsed in 10 days
US macro still solid (IP up, sentiment ~97.5) but October vol, Fed tightening, and a stronger dollar reduce room to escalate
Nov 1 Trump–Xi call set a G20 meeting; talks otherwise on hiatus—best use of leverage is negotiate without new commitments
Midterms flip the House but do not change unilateral tariff power or the bipartisan hawkish consensus on China

US-China joint statement: China agrees to significantly increase purchases; Mnuchin says trade war is on hold.
White House announces US will proceed with Section 301 25% tariffs on ~$50B; truce collapses.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% on ~$200B effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
List 3 takes effect at 10%; China retaliates 5–10% on ~$60B; combined US Section 301 coverage ~$250B.
Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
US exports to China fell from $10.86B (June) to $8.65B (November), about -20% over the window.
Michigan consumer sentiment still high at 97.5 (November), only a modest decline over the lookback.
VIX spiked to 25.23 on Oct 24 and was still 16.36 on Nov 7, up ~27% over the window.

Trump-Xi call cheered markets but advisers said nothing much had changed; talks on hiatus until G20; soybean farmers hurt while steel mills benefit.
Moody's: latest tariffs could cut US growth ~0.2pp and China 0.3–0.5pp next year; List 3 to rise to 25% Jan 1.
Report Trump could tariff an additional $260B as soon as December; List 3 10% scheduled to 25% in January unless a deal is struck.
Democrats take the House, GOP keeps Senate; both parties support a tougher China stance; Oval Office retains unilateral tariff power.
Kudlow (Oct 23): China has yet to agree to US asks on tech transfer and IP theft; leaders will meet 'for a bit' at G20.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the already-scheduled Trump-Xi G20 meeting to reopen talks and seek a pause or delay of the January 1, 2019 lift of List 3 from 10% to 25%, without offering new structural concessions or a large purchase package up front. Keep existing retaliatory tariffs in place as leverage; do not add a new tariff or non-tariff wave before Buenos Aires. Signal willingness to expand agricultural and energy purchases only as part of a matching U.S. standstill, not as a unilateral down payment after the May joint statement collapsed.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is material but not existential. Combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is now about $250B after List 3 took effect at 10% on 24 September, with the rate scheduled to rise to 25% on 1 January 2019 and a further threat to cover remaining Chinese exports (timeline 2018-09-17, 2018-09-24). That sits on top of the April ZTE denial order and the later U.S. government ban on Huawei/ZTE kit—firm-level tech pressure that hits industrial-policy goals even if it is not a full entity-list shutdown of Huawei (timeline 2018-04-16; NDAA ban). Macro already shows strain: the yuan weakened from 6.336 on 14 May to 6.9174 on 7 November (~9.2%), industrial production growth slipped from 6.0% YoY in June to 5.4% in November, and reserves fell about $50B over the window (latest ~$3.08T), with an October drop of ~$34B to an 18-month low as the PBOC defended the currency. That matches the CHN high-threat neighborhood (export hit + FX pressure + firm targeting) but not +1.0: IP is still expanding, reserves remain above $3T, and there is no 2015-style panic. Escalation is the wrong response to this threat. China has already used most of its U.S.-goods tariff ammunition (matching $50B plus 5–10% on ~$60B) while the U.S. can still raise List 3 to 25% and tax the rest of the export book; another Chinese tariff wave would likely invite that response and push CNY toward 7, which Li Keqiang has already said China will not use as a weapon because persistent depreciation does more harm than good. The May 19 purchase-commitment truce was torn up ten days later when Washington proceeded with the $50B action, so pre-committing purchases or structural IP/MIC2025 reform before a U.S. offer on the January hike would repeat a failed bargain. The 1 November Trump-Xi call and G20 dinner create a diplomatic off-ramp, but U.S. officials (Kudlow) simultaneously said they are “not on the cusp of a deal.” Correct stance is therefore engage without new commitments: negotiate a standstill, hold current retaliation, and keep purchase talk contingent on the U.S. freezing the January step-up.
key_factors: US Section 301 now covers ~$250B of Chinese goods; List 3 10%→25% scheduled for 1 Jan 2019
China has already matched $50B and added 5–10% on ~$60B; remaining tariff ammunition is thin versus a possible US expansion to all remaining imports
CNY −9% since mid-May and FX reserves down ~$50B (October drop to 18-month low) — financial-stability constraint on further escalation
Industrial production still growing (~5.4% YoY) so threat is high, not existential
May 19 purchase truce collapsed on 29 May; do not pre-pay concessions
Nov 1 Trump-Xi call and G20 Argentina meeting are a live negotiate/hold window; US signals remain mixed (optimistic Trump, Kudlow not on cusp of a deal)
ZTE denial order plus Huawei/ZTE US-government ban keep tech/self-sufficiency pressure on even if talks reopen

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
China total reserves excl. gold down ~$50.5B over the window to ~$3.081T (latest 2018-11-01).
China industrial production index (same period previous year=100) eased from 106.0 (June) to 105.4 (November) — still expanding, slower.
US goods exports to mainland China fell from $10.86B (June) to $8.65B (November), −20% — Chinese retaliation is biting US farm/goods sales.

Trump and Xi upbeat after Nov 1 call and plan G20 meeting, but US Justice Department simultaneously targeted another Chinese firm; administration has said talks cannot resume until China tables specific actions on tech transfer, subsidies, and market access.
Kudlow: "We are not on the cusp of a deal"; mixed White House signals days after the Trump-Xi call.
Forex reserves fell $33.93B in October to $3.053T, an 18-month low, as the central bank defended the yuan; yuan down ~10% vs USD since February.
Premier Li Keqiang: China "will never go down the path of stimulating exports by devaluing its currency"; persistent RMB depreciation "will only do more harm than good."
